title: The Holy Spirit in my life
summary: The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal "energy," but a Person and God - the third Person of the Trinity. He guides, comforts, convicts of sin, gives power to live, and bears the fruit of character. We come to know him as an ever-present Companion, with whom we can be filled.

sections.heading: The Spirit is a Person, not an impersonal force

items.comment: Peter says that Ananias "lied to the Holy Spirit," and right after: "you have not lied to men but to God." The Spirit can be lied to - and you can lie to a person, not to energy. And he is called God.

questions.text: What follows from the fact that "lying to the Spirit" is called directly "lying to God"?

items.comment: Jesus promises "another Comforter" - someone like himself, who "will remain with you forever." The Spirit is a second Advocate, a personal Companion, not an indefinite force.

questions.text: Since the Spirit is "another Comforter" in the likeness of Jesus, what picture of the Spirit does this build?

items.label: "Comforter" - the same title as Jesus
items.content: The Greek *parakletos* (John 14:16, 26; 16:7) literally means "one called to help" and is variously translated as Comforter, Advocate, Helper, Defender. The same word is used of Jesus in 1 John 2:1 ("we have an Advocate with the Father"). Calling the Spirit "another (Greek *allos* - another of the same kind) Comforter" indicates that he is a Person equal to Jesus and acts as he does - not an impersonal influence.

questions.text: What follows from the fact that the Spirit and Jesus are described by the same word, "Advocate/Comforter"?

items.comment: The Spirit "speaks," "hears," "guides," and "glorifies" Jesus. These are the actions of a conscious and active person, who moreover always directs attention toward Christ.

questions.text: Which of these actions of the Spirit (speaks, guides, points to Jesus) do you need most today?

items.comment: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit." You can only grieve someone who loves and has feelings - a strong proof that the Spirit is a Person in relationship with us.

questions.text: What does it say about the relationship with the Spirit that he can be "grieved," and not merely "used"?

items.label: "sealed" with the Spirit (Eph 4:30; 1:13)
items.content: In the same verse it says that we have been "sealed" with the Spirit (Greek *sphragis* - a seal). A seal in antiquity signified ownership and protection: it marked whom something belonged to, and secured a shipment. The Spirit is therefore God's "mark of ownership" on the believer - a testimony that I belong to God, and a guarantee of security. That is why "grieving" the Spirit is not a threat of losing salvation, but wounding Someone who loves me and to whom I belong.

items.comment: The Spirit "intercedes for us," knows our weaknesses, and "pleads on our behalf." This is the portrait of someone close, who understands and advocates, not of an impersonal force.

questions.text: What does it give you to know that when you do not know how to pray, Someone is praying in you and for you?

sections.heading: The Spirit is God (and God is one in three Persons)

items.comment: Baptism is "in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." One name, three Persons - the foundation of faith in the Trinity: one God in three Persons.

questions.text: Why does it matter that the text says "in the name" (singular), and not "in the names" of three separate gods?

items.label: "Trinity": one God in three Persons
items.content: The word "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible, but the teaching follows from setting texts side by side: there is one God (Deut 6:4), and at the same time the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are each called God and act personally. Formulas such as Matt 28:19 (one "name" - three Persons) and 2 Cor 13:13 (a shared blessing) hold both truths together at once. Scripture confesses the full deity of the Spirit as the third Person of the Godhead - not as an emanation or a lesser being.

questions.text: Why does it matter for a relationship with God whether the Spirit is "the power of God" or "God, a Person" whom you can know and love?

items.comment: The blessing joins "the grace of Jesus, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit." Three Persons act together for our salvation.

questions.text: What does it mean to you that God - Father, Son, and Spirit - engages in your life together, with each Person?

items.comment: Already in the Bible's first sentences "the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters" at the work of creation. The Spirit is present and active from the very beginning - this is the working of God.

questions.text: What does it tell us about the Spirit that he is present and active already at the creation of the world, rather than appearing only in the New Testament?

items.label: "Spirit" also means "breath" and "wind"
items.content: The Hebrew *ruach* and the Greek *pneuma* mean at once "spirit," "breath," and "wind." Hence the biblical images of the Spirit: wind (John 3:8), life-giving breath (Gen 2:7; Ezek 37), the breath of Jesus on the disciples (John 20:22). This range of meaning does not imply "impersonality" - it describes the life-giving, invisible, yet real working of God. The Spirit's personhood is established by the actions attributed to him (he speaks, guides, is grieved), not by the word's root.

items.comment: "Where shall I flee from your Spirit?" - the Spirit is omnipresent, which is a property of God alone. This is a poetic confession of his deity.

questions.text: How does it change daily life to be aware that there is no place or moment where God's Spirit is not with you?

sections.heading: The Comforter who guides, comforts, and convicts

items.comment: The Spirit will "teach all things" and "remind" us of Jesus' words. He is the inner Teacher who helps us understand and remember God's Word.

questions.text: What do you most need to learn, or to be "reminded" of by God, in this present time?

items.comment: The Spirit will "convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment." Convicting of sin is not accusation, but a gentle awakening of the conscience toward salvation.

questions.text: How does God's "conviction of sin" (which leads to hope) differ from a condemning voice that only drags you down?

items.label: "sin against the Spirit": should I be afraid?
items.content: Jesus speaks of the "unforgivable" sin - blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28-29). In context this is about a persistent, deliberate, and final rejection of the very Spirit who convicts of sin and draws us to God - until a person silences his voice entirely. Paradoxically, the very anxiety "have I committed that sin?" is a sign that the Spirit is still at work in you. Whoever despairs at having grieved him is precisely hearing his voice - the door of return is open.

questions.text: Why is the very concern "has the Spirit left me?" rather a proof of his working than of his absence?

items.comment: "All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God." Being led by the Spirit is a mark of belonging to God's family.

questions.text: How do you recognize in practice that you are being "led" by the Spirit, and not just by your own plans?

items.comment: The Spirit "testifies to our spirit that we are children of God" and lets us cry out "Abba, Father." It is he who gives inner assurance and a sense of closeness to God.

questions.text: What would it mean for you to have an inner assurance, given by the Spirit, that you are a child of God?

items.label: "Abba": the tenderest word for "Daddy" (Rom 8:15)
items.content: *Abba* is an Aramaic, everyday, family word by which a child addressed their father - close to our "daddy." It is the very word with which Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). That the Spirit puts exactly this word on our lips (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6) shows the aim of his working: not a servile fear, but a child's intimacy with God. The Spirit does not make us religious employees, but children in the Father's house.

items.comment: "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you." The gift of the Spirit is the way in which the present Jesus is always with us - comfort, not orphanhood.

questions.text: How does the promise that through the Spirit Jesus himself is "with you" every day change the sense of loneliness?

sections.heading: The power and fruit of the Spirit

items.comment: "You will receive power from the Holy Spirit... and you will be my witnesses." The Spirit gives power not for show, but for living and speaking about Jesus.

questions.text: Where specifically would you find the Spirit's "power" useful - for change, for perseverance, for speaking about your faith?

items.comment: "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience..." This is not a list of tasks to accomplish, but fruit that the Spirit bears in a life yielded to him.

questions.text: Which "fruit of the Spirit" would you most want to see ripening in your character - and why that one?

items.label: the "fruit" (singular) of the Spirit, not a list of achievements
items.content: In Gal 5:22 "fruit" is in the singular, even though there are many qualities - this is one, coherent character of Christ shaped by the Spirit, not a set of separate "skills." It differs from the "gifts of the Spirit" (1 Cor 12), which are varied and distributed for service. The fruit testifies to a relationship and a transformed heart; the gifts serve the community. Fruit is not "manufactured" - it is borne by a life that abides in the Spirit (cf. John 15:4-5).

questions.text: What follows from the fact that the "fruit of the Spirit" is one (a character), and not a list of achievements to be gained separately?

items.comment: "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." Victory over evil is not gritting your teeth, but "walking" in closeness with the Spirit.

questions.text: How does fighting evil "in your own strength" differ from "walking by the Spirit"?

items.comment: The same Spirit who raised Jesus "gives life" to believers. The power available in us is the power of the resurrection - the greatest power the universe knows.

questions.text: What does it mean for daily life that the same power which defeated death dwells in the believer?

sections.heading: How to be filled with the Spirit

items.comment: Jesus assures us: the Father "will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him." The first step is simple - to ask. The gift is sure, because it is the promise of a good Father.

questions.text: What holds you back from the simple request "Father, fill me with your Spirit"? What would change if you spoke it?

items.comment: "Be filled with the Spirit" - present tense, ongoing. This is not a one-time "charge," but a daily, repeated opening of oneself to God.

questions.text: How could you practically "be filled" every day, rather than just ask once and forget about it?

items.comment: On the day of Pentecost the disciples, "continuing with one accord" and in prayer, are "filled with the Spirit." The filling is bound up with community, waiting, and openness.

questions.text: What role, according to this account, do community and patient waiting on God play in being filled with the Spirit?

items.label: Pentecost: harvest and the reversal of Babel
items.content: Pentecost (Greek for the "fiftieth" day) is the Jewish Feast of Weeks (Shavuot) - a festival of harvest and firstfruits, celebrated 50 days after Passover. The symbolism is fitting: after the "firstfruits" of Jesus' resurrection come the firstfruits of a great spiritual harvest. What is more, when people from many nations hear the Gospel each in their own language, it is like a reversal of the confusion at the tower of Babel (Gen 11): the Spirit does not divide, but unites humanity around Christ.

items.comment: Jesus invites: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" - and he says this about the Spirit. The filling begins with thirst and coming to him.

questions.text: How great is your "thirst" for God today? What creates in a person the hunger that the Spirit wants to satisfy?

items.label: your body, a temple of the Spirit (1 Cor 6:19)
items.content: Paul calls the believer's body "a temple of the Holy Spirit." In the Old Testament the glory of God dwelt in the Jerusalem temple; now the Spirit dwells in a person. This has two consequences: extraordinary dignity (God chose me as his dwelling) and responsibility (how I treat the body and life that has become his sanctuary). The filling with the Spirit is therefore not a momentary "recharge," but God's permanent dwelling in daily life.

questions.text: What does it change in caring for your body and daily life to be aware that they are a "temple" in which the Spirit dwells?

application.text: The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal energy to be "used," but a Person and God - the third Person of the Trinity - whom you can know, love, and even grieve. It is he who makes the present Jesus near every day: he guides, comforts, gently convicts of sin toward hope, gives power to live, and bears in us the fruit of Christ's character. New life is therefore not an effort done alone - it is a cooperation with Someone who dwells in me and wants to fill me.
application.challenge: Each day this week, begin the day with the simple request from Luke 11:13: "Father, fill me today with your Spirit" - and consciously invite him into one specific situation (a conversation, a decision, a temptation). In the evening, write down one "fruit" (e.g. patience, peace, courage to witness) in which you recognize the working of the Spirit, and not just your own effort. If you notice that you have "grieved" him (Eph 4:30), return at once and entrust it to God.
